title: Pod scheduling queue starvation + CNI MTU mismatch triage
body:
Summary:

This doc captures on-call notes and a preliminary triage for a multi-symptom outage observed in prod clusters on 2025-09-12 03:45-06:10 UTC. User-facing impact: ~15% of API requests returned 5xx due to pod readiness/liveness transitions and spikes in pod Pending state. Root causes appear to be a confluence of scheduler queue starvation under high API server latency and intermittent CNI MTU mismatch on a subset of nodes (bare-metal racks in eu-west-2).

Why this matters:
- Pods stayed in Pending for minutes even when nodes had allocatable CPU/Memory free.
- Some pods became 'Ready' then flapped and failed liveness checks because containers could not reach the health endpoint consistently (TCP resets/fragmented packets).
- We saw a secondary spike in API-server request latencies correlating with heavy scheduler activity and etcd compaction stalls.

High-level timeline (UTC):
- 03:40: baseline: normal traffic, small rolling deploy in hosted-api service.
- 03:45: increase in Pending pods across multiple namespaces; scheduler backlog grows from ~20 -> 120.
- 03:47: alerts: kube-scheduler P95 latency > 350ms, apiserver 95th latency > 400ms, and pod readiness flaps begin.
- 03:50-04:10: intermittent packet loss/fragmentation errors seen via tcpdump on node-nnn (eu-west-2-rack3), multiple pods report repeated TCP timeouts to local DNS and health endpoints.
- 04:05: SREs drain a suspect node (node-nnn) and replace; immediate reduction in networking errors but scheduler backlog only slowly decays.
- 04:25: etcd leader rotates after prolonged compaction-related IO stall on etcd-2; apiserver latency improves gradually.
- 05:00: scheduler queue returns to normal; most previously pending pods get scheduled.
- 06:10: incident declared resolved for page-on-call; several follow-ups opened.

Observations and evidence collected:
- Scheduler metrics: scheduler_queue_length peaked at ~140; active work queue processing fell behind due to bursts of scheduling attempts and retries. kube-scheduler logs show repeated binder lock contention timestamps around 03:46-03:52.
- Apiserver traces: a tail of long-serving requests (LIST/GET on endpoints/endpointslices) that pushed apiserver CPU and created request queuing.
- Node networking: tcpdump on node-nnn shows IP fragmentation and occasional MTU-related ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages; calico/node logs show frequent ephemeral interface re-creations.
- Kubelet: some kubelet logs contained warnings about cni plugin timeouts (~5s) while configuring pod network. Those timeouts caused kubelet to retry pod lifecycle steps and report NotReady.
- Etcd: compaction spike and temporary write latency increase on etcd-2 correlated with a control-plane I/O saturation window (we later learned a backup job overlapped). Disk IO wait was high (iowait > 70%).

Immediate mitigations performed during incident:
- Evacuated node-nnn (drain --ignore-daemonsets) to remove potentially misconfigured NICs; network errors on remaining nodes in rack dropped ~80%.
- Scoped rollback of the rolling deploy in hosted-api (paused) to reduce churn of controller-driven scheduling churn (ReplicaSet controller requeues).
- Temporarily increased kube-scheduler QPS burst/parallelism config (kube-scheduler flags) on the control-plane tier to allow more worker routines while apiserver recovered (note: this is a short-term tweak; we reverted later).
- Triggered emergency snapshot of etcd to preserve state prior to compaction; increased monitoring on etcd disk latencies; cancelled scheduled backup that ran concurrent to compaction process.

Root cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) Primary: CNI MTU mismatch on a subset of bare-metal nodes (eu-west-2-rack3) produced packet fragmentation and intermittent TCP failures. This caused kubelet CNI timeouts, repeated pod network re-attachments, and readiness flaps. The increased churn produced higher scheduling load and retries which pushed scheduler queue and exposed apiserver/etcd latency edges.
2) Contributing: a scheduled backup/compaction process overlapped with peak control-plane load and caused etcd/disk IO stalls which amplified apiserver latencies and increased request queuing.
3) Secondary: controller churn (a microservice with low-ttl pods in the rolling deploy) multiplied scheduling attempts; the combination of controller requeues + kubelet retries amplified scheduler pressure.

Evidence supporting hypothesis 1:
- Packets captured show fragmentation, ICMP PMTUD messages indicating incorrect MTU path.
- Nodes affected cluster to rack mapping: only nodes on rack3 showed calico IPAM overlap and MTU setting mismatch (9000 vs 1500) after an earlier maintenance change.
- Kubelet CNI timeout logs from those nodes specifically.

Evidence supporting hypothesis 2:
- Disk I/O metrics on etcd-2 show sustained >90% utilization during compaction window 03:49-04:18.
- Backup job (snapshot script) started at 03:48 per cron logs; it was not supposed to run during heavy compaction but scheduling drift caused overlap.

Action items (short-term, owners):
- SRE: audit bare-metal node provisioning playbooks for MTU/Calico settings and apply a corrective configuration to rack3 (owner: Liam O'Connor, due: 2025-09-18).
- Infra: add automated post-maintenance validation to check MTU consistency across nodes (owner: Evan Chen, due: 2025-10-01).
- SRE: add a pre-check in backup/compaction cron to abort if etcd latency > X ms or if apiserver QPS > threshold (owner: Maya Patel, due: 2025-09-20).
- Platform: create a scheduler runbook entry for 'queue-starvation' that enumerates steps to identify binder contention, how to scale scheduler worker count safely, and how to throttle controller loops (owner: Sofia Ramirez, due: 2025-09-25).

Longer-term follow-ups (postmortem recommendations):
- Harden CNI rollout processes: ensure calico manifest includes explicit mtu config, validate MTU via host-level check in daemonset bootstrap. Add canary gating for networking changes.
- Improve controller backoff policies: review all controllers with aggressive requeue behavior (e.g., low backoff base) to avoid amplifying scheduling storms.
- Scheduler resilience: evaluate splitting scheduling processing into priority classes, and implement better visibility into binder lock hold times (instrumentation for lock hold histograms).
- Etcd/backup scheduling: restrict backup compactions to a low-traffic window and implement cluster-wide lock to prevent overlapping heavy compaction. Add disk IO throttling for backup snapshots.

Playbook snippets / runbook additions (draft):
- Detecting MTU mismatch:
  - Run on node: ip link show dev eth0 && ip route get 8.8.8.8
  - Verify CNI MTU: kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/calico-node | grep mtu
  - Quick tcpdump: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -vvv 'icmp and (icmp[0]==3) and icmp[1]==4' -c 50

- Binder contention check:
  - kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/kube-scheduler --since=10m | grep "acquiring bind lock"
  - Scheduler metrics: prometheus query: sum(rate(kube_scheduler_bind_duration_seconds_count[5m])) by (job) / sum(rate(kube_scheduler_bind_duration_seconds_sum[5m])) // look for spikes in bind latency

- Emergency knobs (when scheduler backlog high):
  - Increase --concurrent-schedule-syncs (careful) and --profiling on kube-scheduler; coordinate with platform team for safe rollout.
  - Temporarily pause noisy controllers: kubectl scale --replicas=0 deployment/noisy-worker -n noisy-ns (use sparingly).

Unresolved questions / TODO for postmortem:
- Why did the maintenance change that updated MTU only affect rack3 nodes? Was the playbook targeting a label incorrectly? (investigate ansible/bootstrapping templates).
- Did any other racks receive similar calico manifest but not show symptoms? (compare node-level calico logs across racks).
- Can we reproduce the sequence (CNI MTU mismatch -> kubelet CNI timeout -> scheduler backlog -> etcd compaction overlap) in a staging cluster to validate the causal chain? Plan a chaos test.

Notes on communications and impact: 
- Incident Slack channels used: #inc-2025-09-12, #sre-oncall. Initial on-call paging to Maya at 03:46.
- Customer-facing: status page updated at 04:12 with 'Investigating networking & scheduling issues'; engineering note added to postmortem draft.

Appendix: useful commands and queries collected during triage:
- kubectl get nodes -o wide | egrep "rack3|eu-west-2"
- kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}:{.spec.nodeName}: {.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].reason}
'
- Prometheus queries used:
  - kube_scheduler_queue_length: sum(kube_scheduler_queue_length) by (cluster)
  - apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{verb="LIST"}
  - etcd_disk_writes_in_progress (our internal metric)

- tcpdump one-liner to capture PMTUD failures: sudo tcpdump -s 0 -w /tmp/mtu.pcap 'icmp[0]==3 and icmp[1]==4'

Draft PRs and tickets created:
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/k8s-config#391 - calico daemonset mtu enforcement (draft)
- Ticket: LINEAR ISSUE-8422 - mtusync: add infra validation check (priority P1)
- Ticket: JIRA RED-1213 - etcd backup schedule safety (priority P2)

Closing notes (quick personal):
- This incident felt like multiple independent small failures combining into a large outage. Our surface area is large (networking + control-plane + controller logic) and fixing one alone (node drain) helped but wouldn't have prevented the scheduler backlog. Prioritizing systemic checks (MTU validation, backup gating) will reduce these cross-layer cascades.

-- Maya

Draft history: quick notes jotted during the incident, expanded post-incident with logs and queries. Keep this doc as the working triage until a formal postmortem is produced and ownerships are closed.
